newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Floods turned Polish zoo into watery grave.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Floods turned Polish zoo into watery grave.

text.p: Floods hit Opole so fast that despite frantic rescue efforts the Polish city's zoo had to leave some of its most magnificent animals to die in terror.
A tiger, a black panther, a bear and the zoo's three hippos perished in the July deluge which inundated much of the city and claimed 54 human lives in south and west Poland.
So did two lions and five rare South American maned wolves, including three born at the riverside zoo in a triumph for its breeding programme.
"I can't describe how we felt. We were shattered. Some of the keepers who had hand-reared animals from when they were tiny still feel broken," said zoo director Leslaw Sobieraj.
Downpours over south Poland in early July sent a flood wave coursing north up the Oder River by which Opole stands.
Like the rest of the city of 130,000 people, the zoo had two days' notice of the approaching surge.
But no-one had any idea of its huge scale.
Labouring round the clock, staff, soldiers and volunteers built up flood defences and managed to truck out more than 800 animals, making tough decisions over which to save first.
The very few personnel who were qualified to sedate large animals for transport decided to focus first on herbivores rather than carnivores.

When the wave struck it was 1.8 metres (5.9 feet) higher than the hastily-reinforced dikes, roaring in with such force that it carved channels in the earth and swamped even the zoo's higher areas, where staff had hoped some animals would find refuge.
The humans had to flee. "We had no alternative, we had to save our own lives," Sobieraj told Reuters.
"The lions left behind included a female we reared from a cub with a bottle in my office," he recalled grimly.
The big hippopotamus, which should have survived, panicked and fled into its building, never to emerge.

One of the pair of pygmy hippos stayed in the open aquarium and was probably poisoned by the filthy river water, while the other swam out of the zoo and was discovered in a city housing estate that had been inundated.
"I think the current was so strong it probably smashed him against something," Sobieraj said
SOME ANIMALS SURVIVED BY SWIMMING
Some of the abandoned animals, including a bear, two jaguars and a pony, survived by swimming for some days.
As soon as they could, friends and zoo staff went back in boats to see how they could help, pushing wooden debris into one exhausted bear's cage so it had something to stand on.
After days in water the bear was so stressed it refused food but it is recovering, like the other surviving animals.
"There were moments of joy when we returned and found that some animals we couldn't evacuate were safe," Sobieraj said.
"The monkeys were waiting on the high shelves under the roof of their enclosure," he said.
Now the terrain of the zoo, which under Sobieraj had been developing and modernising for the past three years, is a deserted wasteland.

Other Polish zoos have rallied round to help, notably nearby Chorzow which is sheltering 680 of the evacuated animals and birds. Others have taken animals, sent equipment or disinfectants or mounted fund-raising efforts for Opole.
Some animals, including kangaroos, antelopes and lamas have been temporarily housed in garages on a local military training ground, but must move before the bitter winter cold begins.
Sobieraj said the zoo needed equipment for drying out buildings and a generator so they could return by November.
"I have ambitious plans to rebuild the zoo as fast as possible, at least to its former state," he said, estimating the material damage at three million zlotys ($863,000).

But money is tight. Opole, where many residents were made homeless and destitute by the flood that turned apartment blocks into islands, is maintaining the zoo's existing funding for this year but cannot spare anything extra to rebuild it.

Despite their own more immediate troubles, there has been wide concern among Opole's people over the fate of their zoo, visited 115,000 times last year, which was among the southwest Polish city's best-loved leisure attractions in happier times.
Zoo administrative worker Magdalena Hasenbeck said she had been kept busy after the flood by calls from local families offering help and backing the reconstruction effort.
When the zoo appealed for bird cages to aid the evacuation, it was overwhelmed by gifts. One citizen has organised a fund-raising appeal.
Sobieraj wishes the zoo, like the rest of the city and other devastated communities along the Oder, had received earlier, fuller warnings of the deluge.
But he says the zoo's disaster could have been even worse had it not been for the 70 staff and the helpers who pitched in to speed the rescue efforts.
"If anyone had told me beforehand that we should evacuate practically a whole zoo in two days, I would not have treated them seriously," he said.
($ = 3.475 Polish Zlotys)
